lines.text: Everyone must be registered [ingeschreven] in the municipality where they live.
The municipality has a lot of information about you digitally: your address, your nationality [nationaliteit], your bsn, the names of your children, your residence permit.
That is called the Personal Records Database [BRP: Basisregistratie Personen].
If something changes, you must report/declare it officially [aangifte doen] at the municipality.
You must do this if:
you get married or officially start to live together [samenwonen];
you are going to divorce [scheiden];
someone who lives with you has died [gestorven];
you move house;
you go to live outside the Netherlands;
you have had a child.
You make the declaration at the city hall [stadhuis] (in a village, the town hall [gemeentehuis]).
You must always show your proof of identity [identiteitsbewijs (ID)].
Sometimes it can be done digitally, for example when moving — then with your DigiD.
When things change, you usually have to report it quickly: a birth, for example, within three days, otherwise you can get a fine [boete].
Changes in your situation also have influence [invloed] on your rights and duties: the amount of your benefit [uitkering] or allowance can change, for example after a divorce or the birth of a child.
You can also officially acknowledge [erkennen] a child at the municipality.
You can do this if you are not the official parent but do take care of the child.
You then get rights and duties for the child, for example paying for the child.
It can be your new partner's child, or your own child if, as a father, you are not married or a registered [geregistreerd] partner.
You get official documents at the municipality:
a driving licence [rijbewijs];
a passport or identity card.
For an adult these are valid for ten years; after that you must apply for [aanvragen] a new one.
You can also get a passport or identity card for a child under twelve.
The municipality can also help you financially: social assistance, a benefit [bijstand], a waiver [kwijtschelding] of municipal taxes with a low income [inkomen], and social housing [sociale huur].
The municipality can help people with debts [schulden] or very poor people when they need to buy expensive items, such as a washing machine.

Under the Social Support Act [Wmo, Wet maatschappelijke ondersteuning], people can also get other help: household [huishoudelijke] help for old or sick people, transport [vervoer], or a wheelchair [rolstoel] for people with a disability [beperking].
You can ask for help at a care desk [zorgloket] of the municipality or at social neighbourhood teams [sociale wijkteams].
The municipality also helps with social problems: help for lonely [eenzame] people, activities in community centres, and youth care [jeugdhulp].
